newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers face marathon beef talks.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers face marathon beef talks.

text.p: European Union (EU) farm ministers face a marathon three-day meeting from Monday when they meet to thrash out measures to combat the impact of the mad cow crisis on farmers and markets, EU diplomats said on Friday.
"Member states are divided on almost every issue on this part of the agenda and it is hard to see how the impasse will be resolved," one diplomat said.
The Irish EU Presidency said it planned to present a possible compromise paper on Tuesday morning after the 15 farm ministers had expressed their views on Monday.
"But it will be very difficult to achieve an agreement," an Irish official said, adding talks could continue into Wednesday.
Some diplomats and Commission sources suggested that a deal could be struck on a mini-package containing measures having the most immediate impact.
This would include increased purchases into intervention stores, inclusion of young male cattle in the scheme and extension of a calf slaughtering programme to all member states.

Little progress has been made despite instructions from farm ministers at an informal meeting in Killarney, Ireland, in September to resolve disagreements over Commission proposals presented on July 30 to cut output to match falling demand.

EU beef demand has fallen by around 15 percent since a public health scare over Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) was triggered by a British government statement that the fatal cattle brain disease could be transmitted to humans.

The Commission's proposals are designed to bring the beef market back into balance and to finance the 1.3 billion Ecu cost of the mad cow crisis by a controversial plan to cut arable area payments and set aside compensation.
Aid payments to cereals and oilseeds farmers due in 1997 would also be postponed until 1998.
Only Britain and Sweden have so far indicated any support.
But as the European Parliament has not given an opinion on the financing proposal, ministers can't take a formal decision.
Diplomats said it would be difficult for countries, such as France, to agree beef production-cutting measures without a corresponding aid package.

Germany has proposed a different approach which would introduce incentives to beef producers to slaughter animals earlier and at lighter weights, selling the meat on to the market rather than into intervention stores.
But the Commission says the German scheme would be expensive, difficult to control and would not cut production further than its own proposals.
